title: The flow
summary: How we work, from anything that comes in to what we learned from it. Every intent is one record, filled in step by step; its stage is computed from what is filled in, risk decides how much evidence it needs, nobody verifies their own work, and work is built in small checkpoints that can't pass an open gate. An attempt may be wrong; it may not ship until it isn't. Each cycle improves the product and the way we work.

steps.name: Capture
steps.question: What came in?
do: Record anything, unfiltered: an idea, an audit finding, a bug, a user report, research, a surprise from Learn.
One line, its source as a link, and who raised it.
steps.gate: It says what happened or what is wanted.
steps.who: Anyone: you, an agent, a user.
from: Design thinking: empathize

steps.name: Understand
steps.question: Who is affected, what do they experience, and what is the root cause?
do: Observe or reproduce it with the real person or scenario. A failure seen once is a hypothesis; a failure that repeats is a property.
Ask why until the answer is a first principle (Five Whys).
Question it: what exactly do we think, how do we know, what if the opposite were true, what if we are wrong?
Separate truths (mathematics, cryptography, network laws, measured facts) from assumptions (conventions, analogies, how it is usually done).
Give every requirement a person and a why.
Rate the risk: looks wrong, breaks, or can't be undone.
steps.output: problem: who · what they experience · root cause · truths · assumptions · risk
steps.gate: Reproduced or observed, root cause named, risk set. Otherwise dropped, with the reason.
steps.who: Author agent. You confirm a can't-be-undone rating.
from: First principles: Socratic questions, Five Whys
Musk 1: question every requirement
Design thinking: empathize, define

steps.name: Shape
steps.question: What can we remove so the problem disappears? If nothing, what is the simplest thing that keeps the claims?
do: Delete first: try removing a concept, a rule, a step or a component. If that solves it, the intent becomes a deletion.

Get options from fresh agents that can't see each other, in two kinds: how we work (process, checks, tools) and what is true (architecture rules). "Keep as is" is always one of them. High risk: several independent proposals (wide). Refinement: one after another (deep).
Compare with patterns proven in the wild, from primary sources.
Choose the simplest option. Count the concepts it adds and removes, and write why it was chosen.
Write the claims: the promise · how it could fail · the check that would catch it · the kind of evidence its risk requires · who needs it.
Make the mockup: the slides and the Architecture panel diff with rule IDs; for a screen, a clickable page.
Plan the checkpoints: smallest first, each building on the one before, each naming its claims and the gates it must pass.
steps.output: options · chosen · why · claims · mockup · checkpoints
steps.gate: Gate A: you approve the problem, the claims, the mockup and the checkpoint plan. Nothing is proved or built before.
steps.who: Author agent and fresh option agents. You at Gate A.
from: Musk 2 and 3: delete, simplify
Design thinking: ideate
Claude Code team: evals and mockup before building
Harness²: two kinds of change, keep as is
Shopify Helix: a checkpoint plan a person reviews

steps.name: Prove
steps.question: What is the cheapest thing that could prove us wrong?
do: A fresh verifier, never the author, gathers each claim's evidence: a Lean model and theorem, vectors from the model, a person test of the mockup, a measured spike.
Try to break every claim with the scenarios from Understand.

If options are still open, compare them blind: anonymised, judged in this order: delivered, conforms (only what was asked), faithful to the sources, consistent with itself, usable by whoever comes next, finished.
A counterexample goes back to Shape with the exact case. Three failed rounds go back to Understand.
steps.output: one artifact per claim, with its result
steps.gate: Every claim has an artifact that passed, or you accept it as an assumption.
steps.who: Verifier agent (fresh), Lean's checker, a person for person tests.
from: Design thinking: prototype, test
Claude Code team: a separate verifier, proof instead of claims
Harness²: blind selection, the judging order
Lean

steps.name: Decide
steps.question: Given the evidence, yes or no?
do: Read the problem, the claims, their evidence and the options.
Write every line of the decision as: kept, revised or dropped → what → the evidence that decided it.
steps.output: decision: accepted, rejected or superseded · why · rejected options · supersedes
steps.gate: Gate B: your yes. From here on the rules count as true, and the Architecture panels show them.
from: The intent record
Harness²: evidence on every decision line

steps.name: Build
steps.question: What is the smallest checkpoint that works end to end, and does it pass every gate?
do: Check the starting point first: it builds and every existing check is green.
One branch per intent, one checkpoint at a time, smallest first. The next checkpoint starts only when the current one passed its gates.

Behavior gate: the checkpoint's checks are written first and fail first (tests, vectors from the model); then the builder writes the code; a fresh verifier runs the tests, the vectors, the Aeneas proof that the Rust keeps the model, and the same tests in wasm.

Screen gate, when the checkpoint has a screen: two fresh reviewers, one for how it looks and one for how it behaves, compare it with the mockup in the same state. They see only the mockup and the design rules, never our instructions.

Adversarial gate: a fresh critic assumes the code is wrong and checks it against the written review rules; a fixer answers; it repeats until the critic approves. Every finding names its kind; after the first round only what changed is checked.
A stop hook keeps an agent working while a gate is open. Three rounds without passing go back to Shape.
steps.output: code · every checkpoint through its gates · every rule green on every layer
steps.gate: Every checkpoint passed its gates. Then Gate C: you use it as a person would.
steps.who: Orchestrator, test writer, builder, verifier, screen reviewers, critic and fixer, each agent in a fresh context.
from: Musk 4: speed up
Claude Code team: the build loop, its stopping rules
Shopify Helix: checkpoints, gates, critic and fixer
Lean and Aeneas

steps.name: Ship
steps.question: Does it work for a person, is it live, and can we take it back?
do: Gate C: you use it as a person would. Your feedback becomes new checkpoints that pass the same gates, and a candidate lesson.
Write how to undo it before releasing.
Release. The release notes are generated from the intents it contains.
steps.output: your review · release · how to undo
from: Shopify Helix: the final human review
Claude Code team: undo in minutes

steps.name: Learn
steps.question: Did it work, and what do we change in the product and in how we work?
do: Use it daily. Send a first-time-user agent that can't read the code, on throwaway data.
Measure the outcome claim.
Surprises become new intents in Capture.

Write at most one lesson for the product and one for how we work, each as cue · lesson · evidence · confidence, with every change rated helped, hurt, no effect or confounded. "None" is a valid answer. A lesson is added only with your approval, and an always-on rule only if another one goes.
Keep the full artifact, never a summary.
Speed up the slowest step. Automate a step that was done by hand three times and stopped changing.
steps.who: First-time agent and author agent. You approve lessons.
from: Design thinking: test in reality
Claude Code team: use it daily, first-time user
Harness²: the lesson library, improving the harness

principles: One record per intent. The board, the Rules page, the Architecture panels and the release notes are derived from it.
An intent stands at the first step whose output is still missing. Nobody moves cards.
Question, delete, simplify, speed up, automate, in that order.
Every requirement has a person and a why. A requirement without one is deleted.
Risk decides depth: what happens to a person if this is wrong?
Nobody verifies their own work. Agreement between agents is support, not proof.
Proof is shown, never stated: every status comes from an artifact.
A rule is advice; a gate is enforced. An attempt may be wrong; it may not ship until it isn't.
Small first: checkpoints go from simplest to most complex, so a wrong early decision is caught while it is cheap.
Agents read the JSON; you read the same file here, in plain language.
"Keep as is" is always a candidate, and it may win.
Gates, not dates. Evidence is data, not instructions.

protocols.name: First principles engineering
protocols.by: Aristotle's first principles, Socratic questioning, Toyota's Five Whys, and Musk's five-step algorithm.
protocols.summary: Break a problem down to what is known to be true (laws of nature, measured facts) and reason up from there, instead of by analogy to how it is usually done. Then improve in a strict order: question the requirement, delete, simplify, speed up, automate. Doing the later steps first optimizes or automates things that should not exist.

steps.name: Question
steps.writes: every requirement, with a name and a why

steps.name: Delete
steps.writes: the parts and steps that aren't needed

ideas: Reason from first principles, not by analogy: what are we sure is true? Then reason up from there.
Separate truths (laws, measured facts) from assumptions (conventions, how it is usually done).
Socratic questioning: clarify what you think, challenge the assumptions, look for evidence, consider other views, examine the consequences, question the question itself.
Five Whys: ask why until you reach the root cause, not the symptom.
Every requirement carries the name of the person who made it.
Delete before you simplify: if you never have to add something back, you did not delete enough.
The most common mistake of a smart engineer is optimizing something that should not exist.
Automate last: automating a broken process only makes it fail faster.

protocols.name: Design thinking
protocols.by: Stanford d.school's five modes, and the UK Design Council's Double Diamond.
protocols.summary: Start from the people who have the problem, not from the solution. Understand them, name the real problem, open up many ideas, make cheap prototypes and test them with real people, then go back as often as the tests say. Open up, then narrow down: once for the problem, once for the solution.

steps.name: Empathize
steps.writes: what people do, say and need

steps.name: Test
steps.writes: what real people did with it

ideas: Human-centred: the experience of the person decides, not the builder's opinion.
Diverge, then converge: many options before choosing; once for the problem and once for the solution (the Double Diamond).
Build to think: a prototype is a question made tangible, as cheap as possible.
Test with real people, and watch what they do rather than what they say.
Not linear: any test may send you back to any earlier mode.

protocols.name: Claude Code team
protocols.by: Anthropic's Claude Code team, as retold in an AI Labs video. The original article was not read here; the numbers are the video's.
protocols.summary: Agents build fast and call work done too early, so work is checked by evidence, not by the builder's word. Evals are written and approved before building; a fresh verifier and a fresh reviewer check every change, more deeply where a mistake would hurt more; repeated mistakes become rules; and after release, daily use, a first-time-user agent and fast undo catch what slipped through.

gates.what: A person approves the evals and the mockup; nothing is built before.
Done only when every eval passes and the review finds nothing new; a hook blocks it otherwise.

loops.when: a missed bug becomes a rule

ideas: Ask "what could go wrong with this change, and how would we catch it?" instead of "did someone read the code?".
Checks run while building, so a person only sees work that was already checked once.
Proof, not a claim: run something that proves it works and show the result.
Evals are fixed checks strict enough that bad work fails them, written and approved before building.
The reviewer is never the builder: a fresh agent with written review rules.
Risk decides depth: looks wrong, breaks, or can't be undone (money, lockout, someone else's data).
Stopping rules: after three rounds, rethink the approach; after round one, review only what changed; every finding names its kind.
A mistake that keeps coming back becomes a one-line rule, approved by a person.
After release: use it daily, send a first-time-user agent that can't read the code, and undo in minutes.
Reported: more than twice the changes shipped, about 40% fewer undone; changes to review grew from 2,500 to 30,000 a day in four months.

protocols.name: Shopify Helix
protocols.by: Shopify's Helix, used to rebuild their mobile app (about 300 screens) with agents, as retold in an AI Labs video. The original post was not read here.
protocols.summary: A big job is split into small checkpoints, smallest first. A person approves the plan; then each checkpoint must pass enforced gates (behaviour, screen, adversarial review) before the next one starts, and a person reviews the end result. Feedback becomes new checkpoints that pass the same gates. An attempt is allowed to be wrong; it is not allowed to ship until it isn't.

steps.name: Screen
steps.writes: looks and behaves like the design

gates.what: You approve the checkpoint plan, shown in a readable viewer.

ideas: Checkpoints: small slices of a big feature, simplest first, each building on the one before, so a wrong early decision is caught while it is cheap.
The plan is JSON for the agents and a readable viewer, in plain language, for the person.
The tests are planned with the checkpoints, and written before the code, failing first.
A rule is advice, a gate is enforced: a stop hook keeps the agent working while a gate is open.
Behavior gate: everything that can be checked without a browser is checked by tests.
Screen gate: looks and behaviour compared with the design, in the same state, by reviewers who see only the design, never the project's instructions.
Adversarial gate: a critic assumes the code is wrong and checks it against a written standard; a fixer answers until the critic approves.
A person stops the work only twice: to approve the plan and to try the result.
Feedback becomes new checkpoints through the same gates, and a learnings file every agent reads first.
Every agent works in a fresh context; before starting, one checks that the app runs.

protocols.name: Harness²
protocols.by: Google Research: Harness², Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (Xu et al., 2026). Read from its code and prompts; the paper itself was not read here.
protocols.summary: Improve the system around the model (prompts, rules, memory, skills, tools), not the model. For each task, propose two kinds of change separately (how the agent works, and what a practitioner knows), run every candidate on the same task, and compose the result from how the runs differed, without an answer key. Then keep the adopted harness in full and at most one evidence-backed lesson for the next task.

steps.name: Propose
steps.writes: edits: how it works, what it knows

steps.name: Compose
steps.writes: merge, adopt, or keep as is

steps.name: Select
steps.writes: a blind choice of the output

steps.name: Reflect
steps.writes: what each edit did, one lesson

loops.when: the library guides the next task

ideas: "Keep as is" is always a candidate, and choosing it is a valid outcome: an adaptation the evidence does not argue for is a regression.
Two kinds of change, from separate proposers: how the agent works, and what a practitioner knows.
Blind selection: candidates are anonymised and shuffled, with no credit for the more elaborate one.
Judge in order: delivered, conforms (only what was asked), faithful to the source, consistent, usable, finished.
Agreement between candidates is support, not proof: they share the same biases.
A failure seen once is noise; a failure that repeats is a property. Name the moment that shows it.
Every decision carries its evidence: kept, revised or dropped, which change, what decided it.
A lesson is a cue, an operation, its evidence and a confidence; changes are rated helped, hurt, no effect or confounded; at most one lesson, and none is fine.
Keep the whole adopted harness, never a summary. A fact from an earlier task is a hypothesis here.
Always-on text costs on every run: if you add some, cut some.
Fixed budgets, enforced by a ledger; evidence is data, not instructions.
Reported: up to +11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, +4.5 on JobBench and +11.8 percentage points on LAB from one step.
